docs.title: COMPAS ThreeJS
docs.text: COMPAS ThreeJS is a browser-based viewer for COMPAS geometry. It combines a Python API for building interactive scenes with a Three.js frontend for rendering and user interaction.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The Python backend sends geometry and scene commands to the frontend, where Three.js builds and renders the 3D scene. User interactions such as picking and UI actions travel back to Python as callbacks, allowing scripts and the browser to participate in the same live workflow.

COMPAS Protobuf serializes the messages exchanged through a FastAPI WebSocket server. The same frontend can also run as an embedded TypeScript library without the Python server.

Continue with installation, or see the remote-viewer guide to connect from another Python process.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Plugin and @action in compas_threejs.viewer: a toolbar plugin's Python half, talking to its frontend buttons with @action handlers and send().
  • App.plugins: the viewer's plugins, in toolbar order. The App serves each plugin's built frontend and lists them at /plugins.json.
  • Plugin.hide/show/disable/enable: hide or disable a plugin's button groups, buttons or object actions by id.
  • Plugin.attached(), called once a plugin is added to an App, and App.find_geometry(guid).
  • Workspace-aware plugins: @action handlers get (data, workspace), the Workspace of the browser tab that sent the message; inside a handler Plugin.send answers that tab, send(..., workspace=) picks one, and Plugin.send_all reaches every tab. Button state reaches every tab.
  • Workspace.plugins: the subset of App.plugins a workspace's tabs show, served at /plugins.json?workspace=<id>. Workspace.url.
  • App.on_new_workspace(callback) and Plugin.new_workspace(workspace): set up a workspace a browser tab asks for before it exists (e.g. one a plugin opened with viewer.workspaceUrl), before the tab loads its plugins.
  • Plugin panels: hide/show/disable/enable also take the ids of a plugin's docked panels.
  • Plugin.notify(message, kind): a short message for the user, at the bottom of the view.
  • App.show_geometry_edges(geometry, show=True) / Workspace.show_geometry_edges: outline one object's edges, whatever the scene-wide show_edges.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A picked object's metadata shows its fields in order (sent along as "__order__"); sending it no longer writes into the registered Metadata.
  • App.start sends the theme before the background color, so a background set with dark mode on is kept.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The viewer has no toolbar unless plugins add one, e.g. app.plugins = [Essentials(), Views()] from compas_threejs_essentials and compas_threejs_views.
  • The transform gizmo and object locking are plugin behaviour (Essentials in compas_threejs_essentials); the viewer applies a gizmo edit to the geometry as before.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Fixed the spinner getting stuck after a WebSocket reconnect: spinner messages are now persisted (under a stable obj_id="spinner") like other viewer state, so a reconnecting client sees the current spinner state instead of missing a "stop" it never received.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Bidirectional sync between the frontend and live backend COMPAS objects: gizmo drags/rotations (object_transform), toolbar-added geometry (create_geometry), and material edits (material_edit) now mutate the same live objects a running script sees, instead of only flowing updates one way. See src/compas_threejs/viewer/BIDIRECTIONAL_SYNC.md.
  • Workspace.transform_geometry(geometry, transformation): applies a compas.geometry.Transformation (or Translation/Rotation) to an existing geometry and sends only the small transform matrix to the frontend, instead of re-sending the full geometry - useful for moving/rotating large meshes without a full re-serialize on every update.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Bumped compas-pb to 1.2.0 (within the existing >=1,<2 constraint), matching the version the bundled frontend's compas-pb-ts was upgraded to.
  • Fixed Workspace.remove_object() never clearing an object's Inbox-side registrations (geometry_registry, metadata_registry, object_actions_registry, the guid-keyed buttons callback map, and a removed Brep's brep_viewmesh_registry entry) - only the Outbox's persisted material/visibility slots were forgotten, so any workflow that repeatedly removes and re-adds objects under the same guid (e.g. a viewer that rebuilds part of its own scene, or an object action whose geometry gets refreshed to pick up a new default value) leaked a growing set of stale entries, unbounded, for the life of the process.
  • The bundled frontend is no longer committed to the repository. It's now built automatically at release time from the compas_threejs_ts version pinned in FRONTEND_VERSION, via a new invoke pre-build task wired into the release pipeline (run-prebuild on prepare-release@v1). pip install compas_threejs still requires no Node.js. See FRONTEND_WORKFLOW.md.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Install the released Python package with pip, or clone both repositories when working on the bundled TypeScript viewer.

docs.title: Stable Release
docs.text:
For the latest stable release, you can install compas_threejs directly from the command line with pip:

pip install compas_threejs

Using a virtual environment is recommended.

docs.title: Developer Setup
docs.text: Clone and install the Python package in editable mode:

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/compas-dev/compas_threejs.git
cd compas_threejs
pip install -e ".[dev]"

The built frontend isn't committed to this repo, so the viewer won't render yet. Run invoke pre-build to npm-install the pinned compas_threejs_ts release and vendor its build (no extra clone needed), or see below to build against a local frontend checkout instead. See FRONTEND_WORKFLOW.md for details.

docs.title: Typescript Frontend
docs.text:
The TypeScript viewer lives in a separate repository. Clone it next to the Python repository:

cd ..
git clone https://github.com/compas-dev/compas_threejs_ts.git
cd compas_threejs_ts
npm ci
npm run dev

To rebuild the viewer and copy it into the Python package, run this from the Python repository:

cd ../compas_threejs
invoke sync-frontend

docs.text:
• Python 3.9+
  • Node.js 22.12+ for frontend development

docs.title: Remote App
docs.text: The Remote class allows you to connect to a running App instance from a separate process or terminal and send geometry updates to it. This enables collaborative or distributed visualization workflows where multiple scripts can update the same viewer.

docs.title: Step 1: Start a App Server
docs.text:
In one terminal, start a App instance:

from compas_threejs.viewer import App

# Create and start the viewer
viz = App()
viz.start(show=True)

This creates a server at http://localhost:9001 that will receive updates from Remote instances.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect from a Remote
docs.text:
In another terminal (or process), create a Remote instance to connect to the App:

from compas.geometry import Box
from compas_threejs.viewer import Remote

# Create a Remote instance and connect
remote = Remote(host="localhost", port=9001)
remote.connect()

# Add geometry - it will appear in the App
box = Box(1, 1, 1)
remote.add_geometry(box)

# Don't forget to disconnect when done
remote.disconnect()

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
The Remote class provides the same geometry and visualization API as the App class, including:

  • Geometry Management: add_geometry(), add_geometries(), update_geometry(), remove_object()
  • Materials: Support for all material types
  • Metadata: Attach metadata to objects
  • Camera Control: Set camera position, target, FOV, etc.
  • Lighting: Add and update lights
  • Appearance: Background color, dark mode, edge visibility

docs.title: Multiple Remote Instances
docs.text:
You can run multiple Remote instances simultaneously, all updating the same App:

# Terminal 1: Start the viewer
from compas_threejs.viewer import App
viz = App()
viz.start(show=True)

# Terminal 2: Remote instance #1
from compas.geometry import Box
from compas_threejs.viewer import Remote
remote1 = Remote()
remote1.connect()
remote1.add_geometry(Box(1, 1, 1))

# Terminal 3: Remote instance #2
from compas.geometry import Sphere
from compas_threejs.viewer import Remote
remote2 = Remote()
remote2.connect()
remote2.add_geometry(Sphere(1))

Both the box and sphere will appear in the same viewer window.

docs.title: Automatic Connection
docs.text:
remote = Remote()
remote.connect()

# Use the remote...

remote.disconnect()

docs.title: Context Manager
docs.text:
with Remote() as remote:
    box = Box(1, 1, 1)
    remote.add_geometry(box)
    # Automatically disconnects when exiting the context

docs.title: Connection Status
docs.text:
remote = Remote()
remote.connect()

if remote.connected:
    print("Successfully connected!")
    remote.add_geometry(box)
else:
    print("Connection failed")

docs.title: Message Queueing
docs.text:
If you send messages before the connection is established, they will be queued and sent automatically once connected:

remote = Remote()

# These messages are queued
remote.add_geometry(box1)
remote.add_geometry(box2)

# Connect and send queued messages
remote.connect()  # box1 and box2 are sent automatically

docs.title: Real-time Updates
docs.text:
The Remote class is perfect for real-time visualizations:

import time
import math
from compas.geometry import Box, Point
from compas_threejs.viewer import Remote

remote = Remote()
remote.connect()

box = Box(1, 1, 1)
remote.add_geometry(box)

# Animate the box
t = 0
while True:
    x = 5 * math.cos(t)
    y = 5 * math.sin(t)
    box.frame.point = Point(x, y, 0)
    remote.update_geometry(box)

    t += 0.1
    time.sleep(0.05)  # ~20 FPS

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
1. Distributed Computing: Different processes can visualize their results in a shared viewer
  2. Interactive Development: Keep a viewer open while running different analysis scripts
  3. Debugging: Multiple scripts can add debug visualizations to the same viewer
  4. Collaborative Work: Team members can send geometries to a shared visualization
  5. Long-running Simulations: Update visualization from a background process

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
Remote(host="localhost", port=9001)

Parameters: - host (str): The hostname or IP address of the App server. Default is "localhost". - port (int): The websocket port of the App server. Default is 9001.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
All geometry and visualization methods from the App class are available:

  • connect(): Establish connection to the App
  • disconnect(): Close the connection
  • add_geometry(geometry, material=None, metadata=None, actions=None): Add geometry
  • add_geometries(geometries, material=None): Add multiple geometries
  • update_geometry(geometry): Update existing geometry
  • remove_object(geometry): Remove geometry
  • update_metadata(geometry, metadata): Update object metadata
  • add_text(text, position, size=1.0, color=None): Add text
  • add_light(light): Add a light
  • update_light(light): Update a light
  • update_material(material): Update a material
  • add_ui_element(element): Add UI element

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Camera and appearance properties (read/write):

  • background_color: Background color of the viewer
  • camera_damping: Enable/disable camera damping
  • camera_fov: Camera field of view in degrees
  • camera_zoom: Camera zoom level
  • camera_position: Camera position (Point)
  • camera_target: Camera target point (Point)
  • dark_mode: Enable/disable dark mode
  • show_edges: Show/hide mesh edges

docs.title: How Plugins Work
docs.text:
The viewer itself is a renderer: it shows geometry, lets the user orbit and pick, and talks to Python. Everything else - the toolbar, the gizmo, view presets, drawing tools, panels - comes from plugins. With no plugins, the viewer starts without a toolbar.

from compas_threejs.viewer import App
from compas_threejs_essentials import Essentials
from compas_threejs_views import Views

app = App()
app.plugins = [Essentials(), Views()]  # toolbar order; set before start()
app.start()

A plugin is a pip package. It carries two halves that belong together:

  • a frontend, Vue components and TypeScript, built once into static/plugin.js (and plugin.css) and shipped inside the wheel - users never need Node.js;
  • a Python half, a subclass of Plugin, that serves the frontend and answers its messages.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph wheel["pip package: compas_threejs_myplugin"]
        direction LR
        py["MyPlugin(Plugin)<br/>name, static, @action handlers"]
        static["static/plugin.js<br/>static/plugin.css"]
    end

    subgraph python["Python process"]
        direction LR
        app["App<br/>app.plugins = [MyPlugin()]"]
        server["FastAPI server<br/>/plugins.json<br/>/plugins/<name>/"]
    end

    subgraph browser["Browser tab"]
        direction LR
        page["Viewer page<br/>import map: vue, three, viewer API"]
        plugin["definePlugin({ name, groups,<br/>objectActions, panels, setup })"]
    end

    py --> app
    static --> server
    app --> server
    server -- "HTTP: manifest + module" --> page
    page -- "import()" --> plugin
    plugin <-- "WebSocket: channel.send / Plugin.send" --> app

The two halves share one thing: the plugin's name. Python's Plugin.name and the frontend's definePlugin({ name }) must be the same string - it routes every message between them.

Frontend (TypeScript) Python Declare definePlugin({ name, ... }), default export of plugin.js class MyPlugin(Plugin) with name and static Send channel.send(action, data) self.send(action, data) / self.send_all(...) Receive channel.on(action, handler) @action("name") methods, or plugin.on("name") from outside Viewer access useViewer() / setup(viewer) self.app Control the UI - hide, show, disable, enable by id; notify

docs.title: How a page loads its plugins
docs.text:
When a browser tab opens the viewer, it asks Python which plugins to load before it creates the viewer:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser tab
    participant S as App (server)
    participant P as Plugin (Python)

    B->>S: GET plugins.json?workspace=main
    opt the workspace is new
        S->>P: new_workspace(workspace)
    end
    S->>P: manifest(), for each of Workspace.plugins
    S-->>B: [{ name, module: "plugins/notes/plugin.js?v=…", style }]
    B->>S: GET plugins/notes/plugin.css, plugin.js
    S-->>B: built files from Plugin.static
    Note over B: import() the module<br/>its default export is the ViewerPlugin<br/>run setup(viewer) of each plugin, in order<br/>mount the viewer with their buttons and panels
    B->>S: WebSocket connect
    S-->>B: scene, then persisted plugin messages<br/>(keyed state, hidden/disabled ids)

Some consequences:

  • Shared libraries. The page maps vue, three and @compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts with an import map, so a plugin is built with those three left external and uses the page's copies. That is what makes useViewer() and the UI components work inside a plugin.
  • Cache busting. Each file's URL carries its modification time (?v=...), so a rebuilt plugin is picked up on reload.
  • Order. app.plugins is the order of the toolbar sections and the order in which setup runs.
  • Late tabs. A message sent with a key is kept and replayed to tabs that connect later (and after a reload). Use it for state; leave it out for one-off events.

docs.title: What a plugin can add
docs.text:
export default definePlugin({
  name: "notes",
  title: "Notes",                       // heading of its toolbar section
  groups: {                             // toolbar: groups of buttons, by id
    edit: { clear: ClearButton },
  },
  objectActions: { note: NoteAction },  // buttons in the picked object's panel
  panels: {                             // docked panels, by id
    list: { component: NotesPanel, title: "Notes", side: "right" },
  },
  api: {},                              // what other plugins get: viewer.plugin("notes")
  setup(viewer) {                       // runs once, before the viewer mounts
    return () => {};                    // optional cleanup
  },
});
Part Where it shows Typical content groups Top left: the plugin's toolbar section (one shaded segment per group) ToolbarButtons, popovers objectActions Top right, in Actions, while an object is picked Buttons that act on state.selectedGuid panels Right (default) under the object's panels, or left under the toolbar Lists, trees, forms setup Nowhere Subscribing to Python messages, scene overlays, shared state api Nowhere Functions other plugins call

All ids - groups, buttons, object actions and panels - share one namespace per plugin, because Python addresses them the same way:

notes.disable("clear")   # one button: greyed out, its shortcut stands down
notes.hide("edit")       # a whole group
notes.hide("list")       # a panel
notes.show("edit", "list")

Hidden and disabled ids are persisted, so they also hold for tabs opened later. A plugin that lists its ids in ids turns a misspelled id into a ValueError.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Every message carries the plugin name, an action name and JSON data. The frontend's channel.send reaches the @action handlers; Python's send reaches the frontend's channel.on handlers.

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as User
    participant F as Plugin frontend
    participant A as App
    participant P as Notes (Python)

    U->>F: clicks "Add note"
    F->>A: channel.send("write", {guid, text})
    A->>P: _write(data, workspace)
    Note over P: store the note
    P->>A: send_all("notes", [...], key="notes")
    A-->>F: every tab: channel.on("notes", ...)
    Note over F: the panel re-renders

Handlers are always called as handler(data, workspace). Inside a handler, self.send(...) answers the tab the message came from; self.send_all(...) talks to every tab. A useful pattern, which the ready-made plugins follow, is to let Python own the state: the frontend only asks for changes, Python applies them and sends the whole state back. Every tab then shows the same thing, a reload shows it again, and a script can read and change it.

Outside a handler, send goes to the main workspace unless you pass workspace=.

The Python Half, Explained goes through this in detail: what @action and plugin.on do, in which order handlers run, threads and errors, and where each send goes.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is one view of the app, shown by the tabs whose URL has ?workspace=<id> (main without one). Plugin objects are shared by all workspaces - there is one Notes() - and each message tells the handler which workspace it came from.

flowchart TB
    subgraph app["App"]
        notes["Notes()"]
        draw["Draw()"]
    end
    main["Tab: main<br/>Workspace.plugins = all with in_main"]
    beam["Tab: ?workspace=beam<br/>Workspace.plugins = [notes]"]
    notes <--> main
    draw <--> main
    notes <--> beam
  • Workspace.plugins picks the plugins a workspace shows; by default all of App.plugins.
  • A plugin with in_main = False is left out of the main workspace - for an editor that only makes sense in its own tab.
  • A plugin's frontend can open another workspace in a new tab with window.open(viewer.workspaceUrl(id)); Python prepares it in Plugin.new_workspace.

docs.title: Plugins that use each other
docs.text: A plugin's api is what other plugins get from viewer.plugin(name), e.g. a drawing plugin's tool controller. Ask for it when needed, not in setup, since plugins are set up in order. Plugins can also share viewer.state.snap: one writes the snap steps, others follow them.

docs.title: What the viewer gives a plugin
docs.text:
The frontend API is deliberately small. useViewer() (inside a component) and setup(viewer) give a PluginViewer:

state reactive selectedGuid, theme, pickerEnabled, interacting, snap selection clear(), onChange(listener) objects hide, showAll, setPickable, commitTransform, getMaterial, setMaterial camera get, set, setView(preset) channel(name) send, on - prefer useChannel(name) in components notify(message, { kind, key, progress }) a short message at the bottom of the view; with progress (0-1) a progress bar, kept until a notice with its key replaces it plugin(name), workspace, workspaceUrl(id) other plugins, workspaces three closer to the scene for interactive tools: camera, canvas, object(guid), addOverlay, pointerRay, beginInteraction, pauseNavigation, addPickGuard, ...

The Frontend Half, Explained goes through it in detail: loading, when components are mounted, messages, shortcuts, and an interactive tool built on beginInteraction.

useShortcuts({ key: handler }) binds keys while a component is mounted. ToolbarButton, Button, Popover, Tooltip, Slider, Select, Checkbox, NumberField and Kbd make a plugin look like the rest of the viewer.

docs.title: Ready-made plugins
docs.text:
Package Plugin What it adds compas_threejs_essentials Essentials() picker, move/rotate/scale gizmo, hide/lock, theme, screenshot compas_threejs_views Views() view presets and saved views, kept in Python compas_threejs_draw Draw() drawing tools: lines, shapes, extrude, snapping compas_threejs_layers Layers() a layers panel compas_threejs_io IO() glTF/GLB export and import compas_threejs_pixels Pixels() a PDF or image plan as an underlay compas_threejs_wizard Wizard() a first-run tour

To write your own, follow the tutorial.

docs.title: The Frontend Half, Explained
docs.text:
This page goes through the TypeScript half of a plugin step by step: what definePlugin returns, how the page loads it, when each component is mounted, how messages reach channel.on, and how Python's hide and disable reach a button. It ends with an interactive tool built on beginInteraction.

It is the counterpart of The Python Half, Explained. The examples use the Notes plugin from the tutorial.

docs.title: definePlugin: a plain object
docs.text:
export default definePlugin({
  name: "notes",
  groups: { edit: { clear: ClearButton } },
  setup(viewer) { /* ... */ },
});

definePlugin does nothing at run time. This is all of it:

export function definePlugin(plugin: ViewerPlugin): ViewerPlugin {
  return plugin;
}

It exists for TypeScript: wrapping the object checks every field against the ViewerPlugin type and completes the field names in your editor. What the viewer needs is the module's default export: an object with a name, and optionally title, groups, objectActions, panels, api and setup.

So a plugin module is just an ES module:

plugin.js
├── imports "vue", "three", "@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts"   (left external, see below)
├── your components, compiled
└── export default { name: "notes", groups: {...}, setup() {...} }

docs.title: From module to screen
docs.text:
When a tab opens, the page loads each plugin listed in plugins.json, then creates the viewer with all of them:

flowchart TB
    A["fetch plugins.json?workspace=…"] --> B
    subgraph load["for each entry, in order"]
        B["add <link> for plugin.css"] --> C["import(plugin.js)"]
        C -- "ok" --> D["keep module.default"]
        C -- "throws" --> E["console.error<br/>Unable to load the "notes" plugin<br/>(skipped, the others still load)"]
    end
    D --> F
    subgraph create["createViewer(container, { plugins })"]
        F["check names and ids<br/>(a duplicate: that plugin is left out)"] --> G["setup(viewer) of each plugin,<br/>in order; keep the cleanups<br/>(setup throws: that plugin is left out)"]
        G --> H["mount the Vue app:<br/>toolbar, object actions, panels"]
    end
    H --> I["WebSocket connects:<br/>scene + kept messages arrive"]

Points to take from it:

  • A plugin that fails to import is skipped, with an error in the browser console. The viewer still opens with the other plugins.
  • A broken plugin is left out, not the viewer. A second plugin with a taken name, a plugin using an id twice across groups, buttons, objectActions and panels, or one whose setup throws, is not loaded; the others are. Each failure shows an error notice and goes to onError (code plugin_error), or the browser console.
  • A failing component or handler stays contained. A button, object action or panel that throws while it sets up or draws becomes a small ! mark; one that throws later (in a click) stays. A channel.on handler that throws doesn't keep the message from the others. Both show an error notice.
  • setup runs before any component exists, once per page, in app.plugins order. What it returns is called when the viewer is disposed, in reverse order.
  • Messages come after setup. A handler registered in setup is in place before the first message from Python arrives, including the kept (key=) ones.

docs.title: Shared libraries: the import map
docs.text:
The viewer page declares an import map:

{
  "imports": {
    "vue": "./assets/vue.js",
    "three": "./assets/three.js",
    "@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts": "./assets/viewer.js"
  }
}

A plugin built with these three left external keeps import ... from "vue" in its plugin.js, and the browser resolves it to the page's copy:

flowchart LR
    page["viewer page"] --> vue["assets/vue.js"]
    page --> three["assets/three.js"]
    page --> api["assets/viewer.js"]
    notes["notes/plugin.js"] -. "import 'vue'" .-> vue
    notes -. "import 'three'" .-> three
    notes -. "import '@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts'" .-> api
    views["views/plugin.js"] -.-> vue
    views -.-> api

One copy matters because Vue keeps its state per copy. useViewer() asks Vue for the viewer the page provided; a plugin with its own Vue asks a different Vue, finds nothing, and throws "useViewer() must be called inside a viewer component". The same goes for three: an object made with another copy of Three.js isn't a scene object to the page's renderer.

Any other library (icons, a date library, ...) is bundled into plugin.js as usual.

docs.title: Components and useViewer
docs.text:
Components reach the viewer through Vue's provide/inject. The page provides the PluginViewer once for the whole app, and each button slot adds its own state:

flowchart TB
    app["Vue app<br/>provides PluginViewer"] --> toolbar["Toolbar"]
    app --> actions["Object actions"]
    app --> panels["Panels"]
    toolbar --> slot1["ToolbarSlot (notes/clear)<br/>provides { enabled }"]
    slot1 --> btn["ClearButton<br/>useViewer() · useChannel() · useShortcuts()"]
    panels --> slot2["ToolbarSlot (notes/list)<br/>provides { enabled }"]
    slot2 --> panel["NotesPanel<br/>useViewer()"]

useViewer, useChannel and useShortcuts use inject, and Vue only allows that while a component is being set up: at the top level of <script setup>, before any await.

<script setup lang="ts">
const viewer = useViewer();            // ✓ top level
const channel = useChannel("notes");   // ✓

function onClick() {
  const viewer = useViewer();          // ✗ throws: not during setup
}
</script>

Call them once at the top and use the results anywhere. In a plugin's setup(viewer) there is no component: the viewer is the argument, and viewer.channel(name) replaces useChannel.

docs.title: When each part is mounted
docs.text:
A component's state lives as long as it is mounted, and so do the handlers it registers. The parts of a plugin are mounted at different times:

Part Mounted Unmounted setup runs once, before the viewer mounts its cleanup runs when the viewer is disposed groups buttons at start while Python hides the button or its group objectActions while an object is picked when nothing is picked, or while hidden panels at start while hidden - folding a panel keeps it mounted

A disabled part stays mounted, greyed out and inert.

This decides where to keep state and where to listen:

  • State shared by components, or that must survive a remount goes in a module, outside any component - like notes.ts:

    export const notes = ref<Note[]>([]);   // one per page, for every component

  • Listening for state Python keeps (send(..., key=...)) goes in setup. An object action listening for it itself would be mounted only after the user picks something - long after the kept message arrived, and it isn't sent again.

  • Listening for events meant for one component can stay in the component with useChannel, which unsubscribes when the component unmounts.

docs.title: Sending
docs.text:
const channel = useChannel("notes");
const sent = channel.send("write", { guid, text });

send serialises data as JSON and returns true if the message left. While the WebSocket isn't open, it returns false and the message is dropped, not queued. Sending is fire-and-forget: there is no reply to await. Python answers, if it does, as a separate message.

docs.title: Receiving
docs.text:
const unsubscribe = viewer.channel("notes").on("notes", (data) => {
  notes.value = data as Note[];
});

Handlers are kept per plugin/action. When a message from Python arrives, the viewer calls every handler of that pair, in the order they were added, with the decoded data. A message that arrives with no handler for it is lost: there is no buffer.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Notes (Python)
    participant R as Viewer
    participant S as setup handler
    participant C as component (useChannel)

    P->>R: {dispatch: "plugin", plugin: "notes",<br/>action: "notes", data: [...]}
    Note over R: handlers["notes/notes"]
    R->>S: handler(data)
    R->>C: handler(data), if mounted
    Note over S,C: notes.value = data<br/>Vue re-renders what reads it
viewer.channel(name).on useChannel(name).on Use in setup, or any code components only Unsubscribe call the returned function (return it from setup) automatic, when the component unmounts

data is typed unknown: it is whatever Python sent, so cast it to the shape your Python half sends (data as Note[]), or check it.

docs.title: Hide and disable: from Python to a button
docs.text:
notes.disable("clear") in Python reaches the button like this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as notes.disable("clear")
    participant R as Viewer store
    participant T as Toolbar
    participant S as ToolbarSlot (clear)
    participant B as ClearButton

    P->>R: plugin_buttons {plugin: "notes",<br/>hidden: [], disabled: ["clear"]}
    R->>T: pluginButtons.notes changes
    Note over T: hidden ids: not rendered<br/>(group or button)
    R->>S: enabled = false
    Note over S: greyed out, inert:<br/>no clicks, no focus, no popovers
    S->>B: injected { enabled: false }
    Note over B: ToolbarButton shows disabled<br/>useShortcuts stands down

The plugin's components don't need to do anything: wrapping each button, action and panel, the viewer's slot handles it. Two helpers also follow it:

  • ToolbarButton renders as disabled.
  • useShortcuts in that component ignores its keys.

The message is kept by the server, so a tab opened later starts with the same state.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
useShortcuts({ n: clear, "?": help });
  • Keys are compared with event.key.toLowerCase(): "n", "escape", "?", "arrowup".
  • The listener is on the viewer's root element: keys count while the focus is inside the viewer, not in another part of a page that embeds it.
  • A key is ignored with Ctrl, Cmd or Alt held, while typing in an input, a textarea, a select or editable content, while the component's button is disabled, and while a plugin holds input with beginInteraction.
  • A handled key gets preventDefault().
  • Shortcuts are bound while the component is mounted. A hidden button has none.
  • Nothing arbitrates between plugins: if two bind the same key, both run. Pick keys the other plugins in your app don't use.

ToolbarButton's shortcut prop only displays the key in the tooltip; the binding is useShortcuts.

docs.title: Interactive tools: beginInteraction
docs.text:
A tool that turns clicks in the view into points (drawing, measuring, placing) needs the clicks instead of the viewer: no picking, no other shortcuts. That is viewer.three.beginInteraction(handlers), which returns a session:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Active: beginInteraction(handlers)<br/>clears the selection, focuses the canvas,<br/>state.interacting = true
    Active --> Active: pointer and key events<br/>go to handlers
    Active --> Idle: session.release()
    Active --> Idle: another beginInteraction()<br/>→ handlers.onInterrupt()

While a session is active:

  • onPointerDown, onPointerMove and onKeyDown get the events.
  • Picking is off, and every useShortcuts stands down.
  • Orbiting keeps working, so the user can turn the view mid-tool.

Only one session exists at a time. Starting a second one ends the first and calls its onInterrupt, so a tool always learns that it has ended.

Here is a complete tool, a ruler that measures between two clicks on the ground plane:

frontend/MeasureButton.vue
<template>
  <ToolbarButton
    tooltip="Measure a distance"
    shortcut="M"
    :active="measuring"
    @click="toggle"
  >
    <Ruler />
  </ToolbarButton>
</template>

<script setup lang="ts">
import {
  ToolbarButton,
  useShortcuts,
  useViewer,
  type InteractionSession,
} from "@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts";
import { Ruler } from "lucide-vue-next";
import * as THREE from "three";
import { onBeforeUnmount, ref } from "vue";

const viewer = useViewer();
const ground = new THREE.Plane(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 1), 0); // z = 0
const measuring = ref(false);

let session: InteractionSession | null = null;
let points: THREE.Vector3[] = [];
let removeLine: (() => void) | null = null;

function start() {
  points = [];
  session = viewer.three.beginInteraction({
    onPointerDown(event) {
      const ray = viewer.three.pointerRay(event);
      const point = ray?.intersectPlane(ground, new THREE.Vector3());
      if (!point) return;
      points.push(point);
      if (points.length === 2) {
        showLine(points[0]!, points[1]!);
        viewer.notify(`Distance: ${points[0]!.distanceTo(points[1]!).toFixed(3)}`);
        stop();
      }
    },
    onKeyDown(event) {
      if (event.key === "Escape") stop();
    },
    // Another tool began its own session: this one is over.
    onInterrupt: () => finish(),
  });
  measuring.value = true;
}

function showLine(a: THREE.Vector3, b: THREE.Vector3) {
  removeLine?.();
  const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry().setFromPoints([a, b]);
  const line = new THREE.Line(geometry, new THREE.LineBasicMaterial({ color: "#e11d48" }));
  const remove = viewer.three.addOverlay(line);
  removeLine = () => {
    remove();
    geometry.dispose();
  };
}

function stop() {
  session?.release();
  finish();
}

function finish() {
  session = null;
  measuring.value = false;
}

const toggle = () => (measuring.value ? stop() : start());
useShortcuts({ m: toggle });

onBeforeUnmount(() => {
  stop();
  removeLine?.();
});
</script>

What each viewer.three call does here:

pointerRay(event) The world-space ray under the pointer, or null while the canvas has no size. The world is Z-up and in the same units as COMPAS, so points can go to Python as they are. addOverlay(object) Adds a Three.js object of the plugin's to the scene. Overlays are never picked, and the returned function removes them. Disposing their geometry and material is up to you. beginInteraction / release As above. release() can be called more than once safely. The onBeforeUnmount releases the session if Python hides the button mid-measure.

Register it like any button: groups: { tools: { measure: MeasureButton } }. The plugin needs three and @types/three as dev dependencies to compile. At run time, three is the page's copy.

Other viewer.three calls for tools of this kind:

Call For object(guid) the Three.js object of a backend geometry objects() every visible backend object, with its guid (snapping) pauseNavigation() stop orbiting during a drag; call the result to resume addPickGuard(guard) veto picks while guard(event) returns true holdObjectUpdates(guid) ignore Python's updates of an object while the user drags it viewportSize(), onResize(listener) screen-space overlays camera, canvas the Three.js camera and the canvas element

viewer.objects.commitTransform(guid, matrix) tells Python that an object moved, which is how a gizmo ends a drag.

docs.title: Plugins that use each other
docs.text:
A plugin can offer functions to others through api:

// in the Notes plugin
export interface NotesApi {
  count(): number;
}

export default definePlugin({
  name: "notes",
  api: { count: () => notes.value.length } satisfies NotesApi,
  /* ... */
});

// in another plugin, at the moment it's needed
const notesApi = viewer.plugin<NotesApi>("notes");
if (notesApi) console.log(notesApi.count());

viewer.plugin(name) returns undefined when this page doesn't load that plugin; the app or workspace may not include it. Ask for it when you use it, not in setup, since a plugin listed later isn't set up yet.

For simple shared settings, viewer.state.snap ({ grid, angle }) is read and written by any plugin. A drawing plugin sets the snap steps, and the gizmo follows them.

docs.title: Without Python
docs.text:
The same plugin object works with the viewer used as a TypeScript library, without the Python server:

import { createViewer } from "@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts";
import notes from "./notes-plugin";

createViewer(document.querySelector("#app")!, { plugins: [notes] });

channel.send then returns false (unless the viewer was given a send option) and nothing arrives on channel.on. A plugin meant for both uses should work without its Python half, or say that it needs it.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• plugin.js default-exports definePlugin({ name, ... }), with the Python name.
  • vue, three and @compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts are external in the build.
  • useViewer, useChannel, useShortcuts are called at the top of <script setup>.
  • Ids are unique across groups, buttons, object actions and panels.
  • State Python keeps (key=) is received in setup, into module-level state.
  • setup returns a cleanup for what it registered.
  • Interactive tools handle onInterrupt and release their session on unmount.
  • Overlays are removed and their geometry disposed.

docs.title: The Python Half, Explained
docs.text:
How Plugins Work gives the overview. This page goes through the Python half step by step: what each decorator does, when your code runs, and what happens to a message between the browser and your method.

The examples use the Notes plugin from the tutorial.

docs.title: The life of a plugin object
docs.text:
A plugin object goes through five stages. Each one calls into your class at a fixed point:

flowchart TB
    A["<b>1. Class definition</b><br/>class Notes(Plugin)<br/>@action marks methods"]
    B["<b>2. Instantiation</b><br/>notes = Notes()<br/>Plugin.__init__ collects the marked methods"]
    C["<b>3. Added to the App</b><br/>app.plugins = [notes]<br/>sets notes.app, calls notes.attached()"]
    D["<b>4. App.start()</b><br/>serves notes.static at /plugins/notes/<br/>(raises if plugin.js is missing)"]
    E["<b>5. Running</b><br/>a tab opens: new_workspace(), manifest()<br/>a message arrives: handle() → your @action methods"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E
Stage What runs What you can do there 1. Class definition @action("...") Mark methods as handlers 2. Notes() Plugin.__init__ Set up your own state, after super().__init__() 3. app.plugins = [...] attached() Send state set before this point; self.app now exists 4. app.start() - - 5. Running new_workspace(workspace), @action methods, on() callbacks Answer messages, send state

Until stage 3, self.app is None and the plugin can't send anything: send and send_all raise, while hide, disable & co. only remember the ids and send them in attached().

docs.title: @action: marking a method
docs.text:
class Notes(Plugin):
    name = "notes"

    @action("write")
    def _write(self, data, workspace):
        ...

@action("write") does one thing: it puts a label on the function. It doesn't register anything, doesn't wrap the function, and doesn't know about any App. This is the whole decorator:

def action(name):
    def decorate(method):
        method._plugin_action = name   # the label
        return method                  # the same function, unchanged
    return decorate

So the decorated method is still a normal method: you can call notes._write(data, workspace) yourself, in a test for instance.

The label is read later, when the plugin object is created. Plugin.__init__ looks at every attribute of the class, and each method carrying a _plugin_action label is added to a table of handlers, bound to this object:

flowchart LR
    subgraph cls["class Notes (stage 1)"]
        m1["_write<br/>_plugin_action = 'write'"]
        m2["_clear<br/>_plugin_action = 'clear'"]
        m3["write, clear, ...<br/>(no label)"]
    end
    subgraph obj["notes = Notes() (stage 2)"]
        table["notes._handlers<br/>{ 'write': [notes._write],<br/>  'clear': [notes._clear] }"]
    end
    m1 -- "Plugin.__init__ scans the class" --> table
    m2 --> table
    m3 -. "ignored" .-> table

In plain Python, Plugin.__init__ does this:

self._handlers = {}
for attribute in dir(type(self)):
    method = getattr(self, attribute, None)          # a bound method: self is filled in
    name = getattr(method, "_plugin_action", None)   # the label, if any
    if name:
        self._handlers.setdefault(name, []).append(method)

Consequences:

Call super().__init__().

A subclass with its own __init__ must call it first, or there is no handler table and the first message raises AttributeError: ... no attribute '_handlers'.

def __init__(self):
    super().__init__()   # collects the @action methods
    self._notes = {}
The method name doesn't matter, the label does. _write handles "write" because of @action("write"). A leading underscore keeps handlers out of the plugin's public API, since users of the plugin call write(), not _write(). Several methods can handle one action. They all run, in alphabetical order of their method names (the order of dir()), not the order they are written in. If the order matters, use one handler that calls the others. Handlers are inherited.

A subclass of Notes gets _write too. But if it overrides _write, the new method must carry @action("write") again: the label belongs to the function, and without it the action has no handler.

class LoudNotes(Notes):
    @action("write")                 # needed again
    def _write(self, data, workspace):
        print("writing", data)
        super()._write(data, workspace)
Each object has its own table. Two Notes() objects are independent, each bound to its own state. (An App takes only one plugin per name, though.)

docs.title: plugin.on: adding a handler from outside
docs.text:
@action is for the plugin's author, inside the class. on is for the plugin's user, in a script, to react to the same messages without subclassing:

notes = Notes()

@notes.on("write")
def written(data, workspace):
    print("a note was written in", workspace.workspace_id)

notes.on("write") returns a decorator that appends written to the same handler table, then returns written unchanged. You can also call it without the @:

notes.on("write")(written)
@action("write") @notes.on("write") Used by the plugin's author the plugin's user Applies to a method of the class any function, on one plugin object Registered when the object is created immediately Runs first (alphabetical among methods) after the class's handlers, in the order added Gets (self, data, workspace) (data, workspace)

Because on() handlers run after the plugin's own, written above sees the note already stored: notes.notes includes it.

docs.title: What happens to a message
docs.text:
Here is the full path of channel.send("write", {guid, text}), from the browser to your method:

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Browser tab (?workspace=main)
    participant S as Server (event loop)
    participant T as Worker thread
    participant I as Inbox
    participant N as notes.handle()

    F->>S: JSON over WebSocket<br/>{dispatch: "plugin", plugin: "notes",<br/>action: "write", data: {...}}
    S->>T: app.on_message(data, "main")
    T->>I: dispatch "plugin"
    Note over I: app.get_plugin("notes")<br/>drop it if the workspace doesn't show notes
    I->>N: handle("write", data, workspace)
    Note over N: remember the asking workspace<br/>for each handler in _handlers["write"]:<br/>handler(data, workspace)
    N-->>F: anything sent meanwhile with send() goes back to this tab

Step by step:

  1. The frontend sends {dispatch: "plugin", plugin: "notes", action: "write", data}. The plugin name comes from useChannel("notes").
  2. The server gets it on the tab's WebSocket, which knows its workspace from the page URL (?workspace=, else main), and calls App.on_message on a worker thread, so a slow handler doesn't block the server.
  3. The inbox looks up the plugin by name. Unknown plugin: logged, dropped. A plugin not in that workspace's Workspace.plugins: logged, dropped.
  4. Plugin.handle records the asking workspace, then calls every handler of the action, in order, with (data, workspace). No handler at all: a yellow log line "Plugin 'notes' has no handler for 'write'".

data is whatever the frontend sent, decoded from JSON: dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, None. Geometry travels as guids; turn one back into the COMPAS object with self.app.find_geometry(guid).

An exception in a handler

A handler that raises is logged with its traceback, and the asking tab shows an error notice: "Plugin 'notes' failed on 'write': ...". The action's other handlers still run, and the tab stays connected. Still, validate what the browser sends, and catch what you can handle, to tell the user something better:

@action("write")
def _write(self, data, workspace):
    geometry = self.app.find_geometry(data.get("guid", ""))
    if geometry is None:
        self.notify("That object is gone", "warning")
        return
    ...

Threads

Messages from one tab are handled one after another. Messages from different tabs may be handled at the same time, on different threads, and so can a script's own code (app.loop, for instance). If a plugin's state can be changed from several tabs at once, guard it with a threading.Lock.

docs.title: Sending back: where does send go?
docs.text:
The answer depends on where send is called from. While handle() runs, the plugin remembers which workspace asked (in a ContextVar, so each thread sees its own); send uses it:

flowchart TB
    q{"send(action, data)"}
    q -- "workspace= given" --> w["that workspace"]
    q -- "called inside a handler<br/>(directly or indirectly)" --> a["the workspace that sent<br/>the message"]
    q -- "called anywhere else<br/>(a script, app.loop, attached)" --> m["main"]
    all["send_all(action, data)"] --> e["every workspace"]
@action("clear")
def _clear(self, data, workspace):
    self.clear()                      # calls send_all: every tab
    self.notify("Notes cleared")      # inside the handler: only the tab that asked

"Indirectly" matters: _clear calls clear(), which calls _send_notes(); any send in there still answers the asking tab, because the call happens while the handler runs.

Method Goes to Kept for later tabs? send(action, data) one workspace, as above only with key= - replayed to tabs of that workspace send_all(action, data) every workspace only with key= - replayed to every tab notify(message, kind) one workspace, as above; workspace="all" for every tab never hide / show / disable / enable every workspace always

Whatever a handler sends reaches the viewer together, when the handler is done. For long work, show how far along it is: a notice with progress= (0 to 1) is sent at once, and keeps its place with a progress bar until a notice with the same key replaces it:

for i, wall in enumerate(walls):
    self.notify(f"Computing ({i + 1} of {len(walls)})", key="walls", progress=i / len(walls))
    compute(wall)
self.notify(f"Computed {len(walls)} walls", "success", key="walls")

docs.title: key: state versus events
docs.text:
Without key, a message reaches the tabs connected right now, and is gone. With key="notes", the server also keeps it, replacing the previous message with the same key, and sends it to each tab that connects later - a new tab, or a reload.

  • State (the list of notes, saved views, which buttons are hidden): send the whole state, with a key. A new tab is then right from the start.
  • Events ("move the camera there", "notes cleared"): no key. Replaying them to a tab that opens an hour later would be wrong.

On the frontend, the message reaches every channel.on(action, handler) of that plugin, in each tab it was sent to:

viewer.channel("notes").on("notes", (data) => {
  notes.value = data as Note[];
});

docs.title: The other hooks
docs.text:
These are methods to override, not decorators. Call super() in attached.

attached(self)

Called by app.plugins = [...], once self.app is set. Send the state built before that point here.

def attached(self):
    super().attached()      # sends hidden/disabled ids set before
    self._send_notes()
new_workspace(self, workspace) Called when a tab asks for a workspace that doesn't exist yet, before the tab loads its plugins. Set workspace.plugins and fill the workspace here - for a tab your frontend opened with window.open(viewer.workspaceUrl(id)).

The App has two decorators of its own, for events that don't belong to one plugin:

@app.on_object_transform
def moved(geometry, transformation, workspace):
    """The user moved an object with the gizmo; geometry is already transformed."""

@app.on_new_workspace
def opened(workspace):
    """Same as Plugin.new_workspace, for a script."""

docs.title: Class attributes, summarised
docs.text:
class Notes(Plugin):
    name = "notes"                                # required; same as definePlugin({ name })
    static = Path(__file__).parent / "static"     # required; folder with plugin.js
    ids = ("edit", "clear", "note", "list")       # optional; catches typos in hide/disable
    in_main = True                                # optional; False: not in the main workspace

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• name is the same string in Python, in definePlugin, and in every useChannel.
  • __init__ calls super().__init__() first.
  • Each @action name matches a channel.send(name, ...) in the frontend.
  • Handlers take (data, workspace) - or (self, data, workspace) as methods.
  • An overridden handler repeats its @action.
  • State goes out whole, with a key; events go out without one.
  • Handlers check their input instead of raising.

docs.title: Tutorial: Build a Plugin
docs.text:
This tutorial builds Notes, a plugin that lets the user attach a short note to any object in the viewer. Along the way it uses every part of a plugin:

  • a toolbar button with a keyboard shortcut (clear all notes),
  • an object action in the picked object's panel (add or edit its note),
  • a panel listing every note,
  • a Python half that owns the notes, so every browser tab sees the same list, a reload keeps it, and a script can read and write notes.

Read How Plugins Work first if you haven't: it explains the pieces this tutorial puts together.

What you need

Python with compas_threejs installed, and Node.js 22.12 or newer to build the frontend. People who install your plugin later need neither Node.js nor a build step: the wheel carries the built files.

docs.title: 1. The project layout
docs.text:
compas_threejs_notes/
├── frontend/                  # the TypeScript half, built with Vite
│   ├── index.ts               #   definePlugin(...): the plugin's entry point
│   ├── notes.ts               #   state shared by the components
│   ├── ClearButton.vue        #   toolbar button
│   ├── NoteAction.vue         #   object action
│   ├── NotesPanel.vue         #   panel
│   ├── style.css, tailwind.css, theme.css, env.d.ts
├── src/compas_threejs_notes/  # the Python half
│   ├── __init__.py            #   class Notes(Plugin)
│   └── static/                #   built by `npm run build` - not committed
├── examples/notes.py
├── tests/test_notes.py
├── vendor/                    # the viewer package, see below
├── package.json, vite.config.ts, tsconfig.json
└── pyproject.toml

The build writes the frontend into the Python package (src/compas_threejs_notes/static/), and pyproject.toml ships that folder in the wheel.

flowchart LR
    fe["frontend/*.ts, *.vue"] -- "npm run build<br/>(Vite)" --> st["src/compas_threejs_notes/static/<br/>plugin.js + plugin.css"]
    py["src/compas_threejs_notes/__init__.py"] --> wheel["wheel"]
    st --> wheel
    wheel -- "pip install" --> user["user's Python env"]

Tip

The quickest start is to copy an existing plugin, such as compas_threejs_views, and rename it. The files below are complete, so you can also start from an empty folder.

docs.title: package.json
docs.text:
{
  "name": "compas-threejs-notes",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "watch": "vite build --watch",
    "typecheck": "vue-tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts": "file:vendor/compas-dev-compas-threejs-ts-1.5.0.tgz",
    "@tailwindcss/vite": "^4.3.3",
    "@vitejs/plugin-vue": "^6.0.8",

docs.title: 3. The Python half
docs.text:
Start with Python: it decides what the plugin is. Python owns the notes; the browser asks for changes and shows what Python sends back.

src/compas_threejs_notes/__init__.py
from pathlib import Path

from compas_threejs.viewer import Plugin
from compas_threejs.viewer import action


class Notes(Plugin):
    """Notes on the viewer's objects, kept in Python.

    The user adds a note to the picked object from its panel; the Notes panel lists them
    all, in every browser tab. A script reads them in `notes` and writes them with `write`.

    Groups and buttons: ``edit`` (``clear``); object action ``note``; panel ``list``.
    E.g. ``notes.disable("clear")``.
    """

    name = "notes"
    static = Path(__file__).parent / "static"
    ids = ("edit", "clear", "note", "list")

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._notes = {}  # guid -> (geometry, text)

    @property
    def notes(self):
        """The notes, as ``(geometry, text)`` pairs."""
        return list(self._notes.values())

    @action("write")
    def _write(self, data, workspace):
        geometry = self.app.find_geometry(data["guid"])
        if geometry is not None:
            self.write(geometry, data["text"])

    @action("clear")
    def _clear(self, data, workspace):
        self.clear()
        self.notify("Notes cleared")

    def write(self, geometry, text):
        """Sets the note of `geometry`; an empty `text` deletes it."""
        text = text.strip()
        if text:
            self._notes[str(geometry.guid)] = (geometry, text)
        else:
            self._notes.pop(str(geometry.guid), None)
        self._send_notes()

    def clear(self):
        """Deletes every note."""
        self._notes.clear()
        self._send_notes()

    def attached(self):
        super().attached()
        self._send_notes()  # notes written before the plugin was added to the App

    def _send_notes(self):
        if not self.app:
            return
        notes = [{"guid": guid, "name": geometry.name, "text": text} for guid, (geometry, text) in self._notes.items()]
        # key: tabs opened later, and reloads, get the latest list too.
        self.send_all("notes", notes, key="notes")


__all__ = ["Notes"]

Line by line:

name = "notes" The plugin's identity. The frontend uses the same string in definePlugin and useChannel, and the files are served under /plugins/notes/. static The folder holding the built plugin.js. App.start() raises if it's missing, with a hint to run npm run build. ids Every id the frontend declares. Optional, but with it notes.hide("clean") raises instead of silently doing nothing. @action("write") Handles the frontend's channel.send("write", data). Handlers always get (data, workspace): the JSON data, and the Workspace of the tab that sent it. self.app.find_geometry(guid) The frontend knows objects by guid; this turns one back into the COMPAS geometry. send_all("notes", ..., key="notes") Sends the whole list to every tab. The key makes the server keep the latest message and replay it to tabs that connect later. Use send instead to answer only the tab that asked. attached() Called when the plugin is added to an App. Before that there is no self.app to send through, so write before app.plugins = [...] just stores the note. self.notify(...) A short message at the bottom of the view, in the tab that asked.

For how @action and notes.on work under the hood, see The Python Half, Explained.

COMPAS geometry is not hashable

Keep geometry in lists or key dictionaries by str(geometry.guid), as above - {geometry: text} raises TypeError: unhashable type.

Three components show the notes. They read one reactive list, which setup fills with what Python sends.

import { ref } from "vue";

docs.title: The entry point: index.ts
docs.text:
plugin.js must default-export the result of definePlugin.

frontend/index.ts
import { definePlugin } from "@compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts";

import "./style.css";
import { notes, type Note } from "./notes";
import ClearButton from "./ClearButton.vue";
import NoteAction from "./NoteAction.vue";
import NotesPanel from "./NotesPanel.vue";

export default definePlugin({
  name: "notes",
  title: "Notes",
  // Ids are what Python hides or disables: notes.disable("clear")
  groups: {
    edit: { clear: ClearButton },
  },
  objectActions: {
    note: NoteAction,
  },
  panels: {
    list: { component: NotesPanel, title: "Notes" },
  },
  setup(viewer) {
    // Python owns the notes and sends the whole list whenever it changes.
    return viewer.channel("notes").on("notes", (data) => {
      notes.value = (data as Note[] | null) ?? [];
    });
  },
});
  • groups maps group ids to buttons by id, in toolbar order. Each group is drawn as one shaded segment.
  • objectActions appear in the Actions panel while an object is picked.
  • panels with a title get a frame whose title bar folds them; side is "right" by default, "left" under the toolbar, or "top" / "bottom" for a row along that edge of the view.
  • setup runs once, before the viewer mounts. channel.on returns an unsubscribe function, which doubles as setup's cleanup.

Subscribing in setup rather than in the panel means the list is up to date even while the panel is hidden or folded. The Frontend Half, Explained explains why, along with the rest of what happens on this side.

docs.title: 6. Use it
docs.text:
examples/notes.py
from compas.geometry import Box
from compas.geometry import Sphere

from compas_threejs.viewer import App
from compas_threejs_notes import Notes

app = App()
notes = Notes()
app.plugins = [notes]

box = Box(2, 2, 2)
box.name = "Box"
sphere = Sphere(1, point=[4, 0, 0])
sphere.name = "Sphere"
app.add_geometry(box)
app.add_geometry(sphere)

notes.write(box, "Check the dimensions")


@notes.on("write")
def written(data, workspace):
    print(f"{workspace.workspace_id}: {len(notes.notes)} notes")


app.start()

Run it: the Notes panel already shows the script's note. Pick an object and choose Add note in its panel; press N to clear them all. Open the same URL in a second tab: both show the same notes.

notes.on("write") adds a handler from outside the plugin; it runs after the plugin's own. Combine plugins as usual - app.plugins = [Essentials(), Views(), notes] - and control them from the script:

notes.disable("clear")   # read-only: the button greys out, N does nothing
notes.hide("list")       # no panel

docs.text:
npm run watch        # rebuilds plugin.js on every save

Reload the browser tab to get the new build: the plugin's URL carries the file's modification time, so the browser doesn't use a stale copy. Changes to the Python half need the script restarted.

docs.title: 7. Test the Python half
docs.text:
Python can be tested without a browser: deliver messages as the frontend would, and read what the plugin sends from the app's outbox.

tests/test_notes.py
import json

import compas_pb
import pytest
from compas.geometry import Box

from compas_threejs.viewer import App
from compas_threejs_notes import Notes


def receive(app, action, data=None):
    """Delivers a message as the frontend's `channel.send(action, data)` would."""
    message = {"dispatch": "plugin", "plugin": "notes", "action": action, "data": data}
    app.on_message(json.dumps(message).encode("utf-8"))


def last_sent(app):
    return compas_pb.pb_load_bts(app.outbox._queue[-1][0])


def test_a_note_from_the_browser_is_stored_and_sent_back():
    app = App()
    notes = Notes()
    app.plugins = [notes]
    box = Box(1)
    app.add_geometry(box)

    receive(app, "write", {"guid": str(box.guid), "text": "Too small"})

    assert notes.notes == [(box, "Too small")]
    sent = last_sent(app)
    assert sent["action"] == "notes"
    assert sent["data"][0]["text"] == "Too small"


def test_an_empty_note_deletes_it():
    app = App()
    notes = Notes()
    app.plugins = [notes]
    box = Box(1)
    notes.write(box, "Too small")
    notes.write(box, "  ")
    assert notes.notes == []


def test_ids_are_checked():
    notes = Notes()
    notes.disable("clear")
    assert notes.disabled == {"clear"}
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        notes.hide("clean")

docs.text: Symptom Cause FileNotFoundError: Plugin 'notes' has no built frontend Run npm run build; check static points at the build's outDir. The section doesn't appear; the browser console says Unable to load the "notes" plugin plugin.js failed to import - look at the error below it. Often a missing default export. useViewer() must be called inside a viewer component Vue was bundled into plugin.js; keep vue, three and the viewer package external. The "notes" plugin uses the id "…" twice: it was not loaded (error notice) A duplicate id within one plugin, or two plugins with the same name. The "notes" plugin was not loaded: its setup failed setup threw - the browser console has the stack. A ! mark instead of a button or panel That component threw while it set up or drew. Plugin 'notes' failed on 'write': … (error notice) A Python handler raised - the traceback is in the Python log. Plugin 'notes' has no handler for 'write' (Python log) The action names on both sides differ. TypeError in a handler with one argument Handlers take (data, workspace). A plugin class looks wrong (no colours) theme.css is missing, or a class is built from strings Tailwind can't see.

docs.title: compas_threejs.viewer.plugin.Plugin
docs.text:
Plugin()

A viewer plugin: toolbar buttons in the frontend, and their Python half.

A subclass sets name and static, the folder holding the plugin's built frontend, plugin.js (and plugin.css, if it has one). plugin.js default-exports definePlugin({ name, groups }) from @compas-dev/compas-threejs-ts, with the same name. A plugin without static is Python only: the page loads nothing for it. Methods marked with @action("...") handle what the frontend sends, and are told which workspace (browser tab) sent it; send answers that tab, send_all talks to every tab.

The plugin is one object for all workspaces: a workspace shows the plugins in Workspace.plugins, by default all of App.plugins - but the main workspace leaves out a plugin whose in_main is False, one made for other tabs (an element's editor).

hide, show, disable and enable take the ids of button groups, single buttons or panels, as the frontend names them in groups and panels. A subclass may list them in ids, so that a misspelled id raises instead of doing nothing.

Examples:

>>> app = App()
>>> standard = Standard()
>>> app.plugins = [standard, Camera()]
>>> standard.hide("display")  # a whole group
>>> standard.disable("scale")  # one button
>>> app.start()

docs.title: notify
docs.text:
notify(message, kind='info', *, workspace=None, key=None, progress=None)

Shows message to the user for a moment, at the bottom of the view.

kind is "info", "success", "warning" or "error". It goes to one workspace, chosen like send's; workspace="all" shows it in every tab.

With a key, it takes the place of the notice with the same key still shown. With a progress (0 to 1) it shows a progress bar, and stays until a notice with its key takes its place - so a long handler can show how far along it is, then how it ended, in one notice::

for i, wall in enumerate(walls):
    self.notify(f"Computing ({i + 1} of {len(walls)})", key="walls", progress=i / len(walls))
    ...
self.notify(f"Computed {len(walls)} walls", "success", key="walls")

A notice with a progress is sent at once, not when the handler is done (see Outbox.batch).

send(action_name, data=None, *, workspace=None, key=None)

Sends data to the frontend's channel.on(action_name, ...) handlers in one workspace.

That is workspace (a Workspace or its id) if given; otherwise, inside an action handler, the workspace the handled message came from, and elsewhere "main".

With a key, the message is also kept (replacing the last one with that key) and replayed to browsers that connect later - for state, like a list of saved views.

docs.title: compas_threejs.viewer.app.App
docs.text:
App(host: str = '127.0.0.1', websocket_port: int = 9001, frontend_dir=None)

The App class runs the viewer server and hosts one or more Workspaces. Each Workspace is an isolated, browser-facing viewport with its own camera, lighting, and geometry; a new App always starts with a "main" workspace, and the properties and methods below are shorthands that forward to it.

Attributes:

  • loop (callable) –

    A user-defined callback function that will be called in each iteration of the main loop.

  • loop_interval ((float, optional)) –

    The interval in seconds for the main loop to run. Default is 0.02 (50 FPS).

  • background_color (Color) –

    The background color of the main workspace.

  • camera_damping (bool) –

    Whether camera damping is enabled. Default is True.

  • default_lighting ((bool, optional)) –

    Whether to include default lighting in the scene. Default is True. This attribute can only be modifief before calling App.start().

  • world_axis ((bool, optional)) –

    Whether to show the world axis in the scene. Default is True.

  • picker ((bool, optional)) –

    Whether to enable the object picker in the scene. Default is True.

  • camera_fov ((float, optional)) –

    The camera field of view (FOV) in degrees. Default is 60.

  • camera_zoom ((float, optional)) –

    The camera zoom level. Default is 1.

  • dark_mode ((bool, optional)) –

    Whether to enable dark mode for the main workspace. Default is False.

  • camera_position ((Point, optional)) –

    The camera position in world coordinates. Default is (8, -15, 15).

  • camera_target ((Point, optional)) –

    The camera target point used by orbit controls. Default is (0, 0, 0).

  • show_edges ((bool, optional)) –

    Whether to show edges of the mesh. Default is False.

frontend_dir : str | pathlib.Path, optional Directory of a built frontend (an index.html plus its assets) to serve instead of this package's own bundled one at viewer/frontend/. Lets a consumer pin the served frontend to its own copy - e.g. one it rebuilds itself from a branch or fork of the frontend source - independent of whatever happens to be bundled in this installed package.

docs.title: Basic Geometry
docs.text: This tutorial covers the various ways you can add COMPAS geometry to the compas_threejs viewer, from single objects to multiple objects with custom appearances.

docs.title: 1. Adding a Single Geometry
docs.text:
from compas.geometry import Box
from compas_threejs.viewer import App

# 1. Create a viewer instance
viz = App()

# 2. Create a COMPAS geometry
box = Box(1, 1, 1)

# 3. Add the geometry to the viewer
viz.add_geometry(box)

# 4. Start the viewer
viz.start()

The add_geometry() method is the core function for adding objects to the scene. It takes a COMPAS geometry object as its primary argument. When you call viz.start(), this object is serialized and sent to the frontend to be rendered. A websocket connection is open for the bidirectional communication between the backend and frontend.

docs.title: 2. Adding Multiple Geometries
docs.text:
You can add as many geometries as you like to the scene by calling add_geometry() multiple times or by using add_geometries().

from compas.geometry import Box, Sphere
from compas_threejs.viewer import App

viz = App()

# Create multiple geometries
box = Box(1, 1, 1)
sphere = Sphere(radius=0.5)

# Add them to the viewer one by one
viz.add_geometry(box)
viz.add_geometry(sphere)

# Or add them all at once
# viz.add_geometries([box, sphere])

viz.start()

The viewer maintains a registry of all objects in the scene. Each time you call add_geometry(), the new object is added to this registry. When the viewer starts, it sends all registered objects to the frontend. The add_geometries() method is a convenient way to add a list of objects in a single call.

docs.title: 3. Adding Geometry with a Custom Material
docs.text:
By default, geometries are rendered with a standard compas-blue material. To customize the appearance of an object, you can create a Material object and pass it to the add_geometry() method.

from compas.geometry import Torus
from compas.colors import Color
from compas_threejs.viewer import App
from compas_threejs.materials import Material

viz = App()

# Create a geometry
torus = Torus(radius_axis=1, radius_pipe=0.3)

# Create a custom material
custom_material = Material(
    color=Color.blue(),
    metalness=0.8,
    roughness=0.2,
    wireframe=True
)

# Add the geometry with the custom material
viz.add_geometry(torus, material=custom_material)

viz.start()
The Material class allows you to control the visual properties of your geometry. Here are some of the key parameters:

  • color: The base color of the material (instance of compas.colors.Color).
  • metalness: A float between 0.0 (non-metallic) and 1.0 (fully metallic).
  • roughness: A float between 0.0 (smooth, reflective) and 1.0 (fully rough).
  • emissive: The color of light emitted by the material.
  • emissive_intensity: The intensity of the emissive light.
  • flat_shading: A boolean that determines whether to use flat or smooth shading.
  • wireframe: A boolean that, if True, renders the object as a wireframe.

By creating a Material object and passing it along with your geometry to add_geometry(), you are telling the viewer to associate that specific appearance with that object. The viewer then sends both the geometry data and the material properties to the frontend.
